ai-at-work.title: Anthropic says it will watermark text generated by its AI models
ai-at-work.excerpt: Anthropic will extend support for watermarking AI generations for older models as well.
ai-at-work.dwp_take: Anthropic announced it will add watermarks to text generated by its AI models, including retroactive support for older versions. This matters because digital workplace teams are increasingly using AI for content creation, and watermarking helps distinguish human-authored from machine-generated work, which has real implications for authenticity, compliance, and knowing who actually wrote that email. Here's the thing though: watermarks only work if everyone actually looks for them, and in my experience, most people won't, so we're still going to spend the next two years arguing about whether that memo came from a human or Claude.

ai-at-work.dwp_take: IBM just committed a quarter billion dollars to provide cloud infrastructure for Together AI, a startup that's building AI services on Nvidia's hardware. For digital workplace leaders, this matters because it signals where enterprise compute is heading: toward specialized AI infrastructure partnerships rather than one-size-fits-all cloud platforms. I'd love to know how many CIOs are currently explaining to their CFOs why they need yet another cloud vendor relationship, because apparently one wasn't enough.

ai-at-work.title: CoreWeave coasts to a solid earnings beat, sending its stock higher after-hours

ai-at-work.dwp_take: CoreWeave beat earnings expectations by a wide margin and its stock jumped 14% in after-hours trading, signaling investor confidence in the AI infrastructure play. For digital workplace pros, this matters because AI compute infrastructure is becoming the backbone of enterprise collaboration tools and workplace tech stacks. Here's the thing though: an earnings beat doesn't mean the underlying business model is bulletproof, so don't get too excited until we see sustained profitability, not just adjusted metrics.

ai-at-work.excerpt: River AI Inc., a startup that helps enterprises customize open-source artificial intelligence models, has raised $1.1 billion in early-stage funding. The company stated in today’s announcement that it
ai-at-work.dwp_take: River AI just closed $1.1 billion in funding to help companies customize open-source AI models for their own needs. This matters because every organization now realizes generic AI isn't cutting it, and digital workplace teams need tools that actually understand their specific workflows and data instead of some one-size-fits-all chatbot. The real question is whether River can deliver on that promise faster than enterprises get tired of waiting, because I've seen plenty of AI startups with big funding and bigger promises crater when reality hits.

tools-tech.title: Why software factories are back - and how they work in the age of AI
tools-tech.excerpt: Imagine submitting your vibe-coded app to a service that validates, tests, and then mass-produces it in a repeatable, automated fashion for delivery to a wide audience.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Software factories are making a comeback as automated platforms that take application code, validate it, test it, and deploy it at scale without manual intervention. This matters to digital workplace pros because it directly impacts how fast your organization can ship internal tools, updates, and integrations that actually get used. Honestly, the irony is thick here: we spent twenty years trying to democratize software development so non-coders could build things, and now we're automating away the developers we trained to use those tools in the first place.

tools-tech.title: How to create flyers with AI that people won't hate: 8 tips (and prompts) that really work
tools-tech.excerpt: Most AI flyers are still a mess, but the right prompts can make all the difference.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone figured out that garbage prompts produce garbage AI flyers, so ZDNet published eight tips to make them actually look professional. This matters because every digital workplace now has someone spamming teams with auto-generated design disasters, and better prompts mean fewer requests for your actual designer to fix them. Here's the thing though: if your organization needs eight tips to not embarrass itself with AI flyers, maybe you should just hire that designer instead of pretending AI is a free substitute for knowing what good design looks like.

tools-tech.title: A developer got Word 1.1a from 1990 to run on Windows 11 - try it yourself
tools-tech.excerpt: Longing for a plain, old-fashioned version of Microsoft Word without all the bells, whistles, and AI slop? One developer managed to coax Word 1.1a to run on today's Windows.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Someone successfully got a 1990 version of Microsoft Word running on Windows 11, proving that ancient software can still boot up on modern systems. This matters because it highlights how bloated modern applications have become and raises real questions about whether we actually need all the features we're paying for. Honestly, the fact that people are nostalgic enough to try this tells you everything you need to know about the state of productivity software today.

tools-tech.title: Linux desktop use surged to 22% on one workday, Cloudflare data shows
tools-tech.excerpt: The Linux desktop's popularity is growing fast, and there are a few reasons why.
tools-tech.dwp_take: Cloudflare's data showed Linux desktop usage hit 22% during a single workday, marking a significant jump from historical averages. For IT teams and workplace tech strategists, this means Linux is finally becoming a real support and standardization consideration rather than something you can politely ignore. After three decades watching this "year of Linux" prediction cycle repeat, I'm cautiously intrigued, but I'll believe it's truly mainstream when I stop getting support tickets about why the printer driver won't install.

digital-culture.title: More than half of workers would take a pay cut for job security
digital-culture.excerpt: Employees in 2026 are seriously worried about how unstable their jobs may be. So worried, in fact, that more than half say they’d willingly swap part of their paycheck for greater job security.Accordi
digital-culture.dwp_take: More than half of workers surveyed say they'd accept lower pay in exchange for genuine job security. This tells digital workplace professionals that employee anxiety about layoffs and automation is reshaping what people actually value, forcing organizations to rethink retention strategies beyond just competitive salaries. Here's the thing: if your workforce is this spooked, no amount of ping-pong tables and unlimited PTO is going to fix the real problem, which is they don't trust you'll keep them around.

digital-culture.title: Meet 21 Black women who bounced back and are thriving after being pushed out of the workplace
digital-culture.excerpt: For Black women, the instability of today’s job market has been particularly severe. Since early 2025, approximately 600,000 Black women have become unemployed, left the labor force, or otherwise been
digital-culture.dwp_take: Fast Company profiled 21 Black women who lost their jobs or left the workforce involuntarily and have since rebuilt successful careers on their own terms. This matters because it highlights a real pattern many digital workplace leaders ignore: systemic inequity in hiring, retention, and advancement that disproportionately affects Black women, and it should make HR teams ask hard questions about their own practices. The fact that these women had to leave traditional employment to thrive says less about their resilience and a lot more about what's broken in how we hire and keep talent.

industry-news.title: Google Drive Stops Automatic Photo Backups to Google Photos on Desktop
industry-news.excerpt: Google Drive has ended automatic desktop photo backups to Google Photos, forcing users to switch to a browser-based workflow to keep folders synced. The post Google Drive Stops Automatic Photo Backups
industry-news.dwp_take: Google killed the automatic photo backup feature in Google Drive for desktop, meaning users now have to jump through the browser to keep their photo folders synced. This matters because plenty of organizations rely on Drive for simple file workflows, and removing friction-free features forces teams to adopt workarounds or find alternatives. I'm not sure who asked for this one, but it's another reminder that cloud vendors love optimizing for mobile and web while treating desktop users like we're living in 2005.

industry-news.title: Ninth Circuit Dismisses Meta, TikTok Appeals in Social Media Addiction Cases
industry-news.excerpt: The Ninth Circuit dismissed Meta and TikTok’s early appeals, keeping thousands of social media addiction lawsuits moving through lower courts. The post Ninth Circuit Dismisses Meta, TikTok Appeals in
industry-news.dwp_take: The Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals rejected Meta and TikTok's attempts to dismiss thousands of pending lawsuits accusing their platforms of addicting users, particularly minors, allowing cases to proceed in lower courts. This matters to digital workplace folks because it signals that courts are taking platform design and psychological manipulation seriously, which will eventually influence how companies approach employee digital experiences and wellness policies. Here's the thing: if Meta and TikTok can't escape liability for addictive design, your company's "always on" Slack culture suddenly looks a lot riskier to your legal team.
